sentences.text: Cladoselache is an extinct basal genus of cartilaginous fish that lived during the Devonian.
Although its body shape resembled modern lamnid sharks like the mako and great white, this ancient creature was not closely related to them.
This predator grew to a length of up to two meters and possessed a streamlined body with a deeply forked tail.
Its tail was tapered and keeled, ending in a crescent-shaped caudal fin.
The animal featured a strange, large mouth located in the center of its head.
The eyes were protected by a ring of more than 20 small dermal ossifications.
Tiny, bluntly conical placoid scales covered the skin but were absent from much of the body.
All fins except the tail had a wide base continuous with the torso and were supported by cartilaginous rods called radials.
Evidence suggests it had at least five pairs of slender, well-separated branchial arches, resulting in five gill slits on each side.
Stomach contents preserved in fossils indicate it ate small ray-finned fishes, thylacocephalan arthropods, conodonts, and hagfish-like proto-vertebrates.
Fish remains found tail-first in the stomachs suggest it was a fast and agile hunter.
It had a weak jaw joint compared to modern sharks, compensated by very powerful jaw muscles.
Fossils were discovered in the Cleveland Shale on the south shore of Lake Erie.
Remains have also been found in Europe.
The genus was described by Dean in 1894, with the type species being Cladoselache fyleri.
The teeth were slender and smooth-edged, adapted for grasping prey rather than tearing or chewing.
The animal likely caught prey by the tail and swallowed them whole.
Its long, slender cylindrical body and tail shape suggest it was a fierce predator that swam quickly and with great agility.
The musculature consisted of discrete packages of muscle fibers that were easier to differentiate than in modern sharks.
It is often described as a basal chondrichthyan rather than a true shark.
Cladoselache is not a member of the modern shark group (Selachii), which evolved later in the Jurassic Period.
Recent studies suggest it is closely related to symmoriiforms based on distinctive traits of its chondrocranium, dorsal fin spines, and pectoral fin bases.
It may belong to an early-diverging clade at the base of Chondrichthyes or Elasmobranchii alongside symmoriiforms.
The creature lived during the Late Devonian period.
It lived from 372.15 to 358.86 million years ago during the Famennian stage.
Early sources suggested it might have had six or seven gill slits, but this has not been confirmed.
There is a debate regarding whether Cladoselache was the earliest-diverging member of Chondrichthyes or an elasmobranch that originated after holocephalans.
Some studies suggested it was a derived elasmobranch close to hybodonts and modern sharks, but this view was considered uncertain and unstable.
An alternative hypothesis suggests it lies on the holocephalan stem-group leading to modern chimaeras.
It is debated whether Cladoselache and symmoriiforms are more closely related to chimaeras than to true sharks and rays.
The method of reproduction remains unresolved, as it lacks known claspers despite other early shark fossils showing them.
